method: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer) 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis' (published 28 December 2021). Every claim is a paraphrase backed by anchors (scripts/anchor.py): verify.py --source re-finds each anchored span in a fresh copy of the source, checks the claim's numbers against it and rejects copying. LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC8814294). The source's words are NOT reproduced here.

claims.claim: **A rheumatologist makes the diagnosis.** MRI helps, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose axSpA by itself.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take a full history and examine:** look for spondyloarthritis features, other causes of back pain, and common co-existing problems such as non-specific back pain and fibromyalgia.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Inflammatory back pain is the key symptom but is non-specific** (sensitivity 74%, specificity 40% in nr-axSpA). Clues: rest does not help, pain at night, and morning stiffness that eases with activity.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider fibromyalgia**, which can mimic, accompany or follow axSpA; about 23% of men and 21% of women with nr-axSpA have it.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Test CRP and HLA-B27 in everyone being assessed.** A normal CRP can become raised later: 50% of placebo-arm patients with a normal baseline CRP had a high one within 16 weeks, so repeat it.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **HLA-B27 together with a positive ASAS MRI makes nr-axSpA very likely** (specificity 99%); with neither, only 2% turn out to have axSpA.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start with an AP pelvic X-ray**, before any sacroiliac MRI; dedicated sacroiliac views seldom add anything. Read it in clinical context, and remember a normal film does not rule out nr-axSpA.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not use CT to investigate suspected nr-axSpA.**
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If suspicion remains, order sacroiliac MRI with T1 and STIR sequences**, no contrast needed.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Sacroiliac bone marrow oedema is not diagnostic on its own.** It appears in 23% of healthy controls and 40–64% of women after childbirth, as well as in athletes.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Repeating a negative MRI rarely helps if HLA-B27 is negative:** fewer than 5% convert to positive.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Classification criteria (ASAS) are not a diagnostic checklist** for individual patients, though their components inform the overall judgement.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Share decisions and educate.** The patient's goals and preferences drive care, and education is a core part of management.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Build in lifelong regular exercise;** physiotherapy may also help.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **An NSAID is the first drug to use**, at the maximum tolerated dose in the studies; it can also help patients take part in exercise.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Conventional DMARDs do not treat axial disease.** Sulfasalazine is an option for peripheral arthritis.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Corticosteroids:** sacroiliac injection has a limited, short-lived role; oral or other systemic steroids have no clear place.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider a biologic only when the diagnosis is secure** and disease stays active despite exercise and an NSAID.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **TNF inhibitors and IL-17 inhibitors both work for axial symptoms** (ASAS40 32 to 57% with TNF inhibitors, 35–42% with IL-17 inhibitors); they have not been compared head to head.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Let extra-articular disease guide the class.** TNF inhibitors suit uveitis (certolizumab cut flares by 87%; etanercept may be worse), IBD and psoriasis. IL-17 inhibitors suit psoriasis but do not help IBD and lack uveitis evidence.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ustekinumab does not work** in nr-axSpA or AS.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **High ASDAS-CRP predicts response to a TNF inhibitor** better than BASDAI; MRI sacroiliitis alone does not clearly predict it.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Avoid stopping a TNF inhibitor in stable patients:** 70–87% flared within 48–68 weeks of stopping, whereas doubling the interval raised flares only from 16.3 to 21%.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Function, work and quality of life suffer as much as in AS** and improve in responders; fibromyalgia, depression and fatigue make them worse.
claims.locator: Australian expert panel, Rheumatology and Therapy (Springer), 'Australian Consensus Statements for the Assessment and Management of Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis', published 28 December 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8814294/, retrieved 2026-09-23
